vignette:
Mele is seventy-five years old, but she carries the heat and terror of a single afternoon from when she was twenty inside her still. For fifty-five years, she has worked diligently as an auditor, a profession of order and logic that stands in stark opposition to the memory that governs her life. The event itself resists language; when she tries to speak of it to her husband, Tane, or now, in the quiet of the therapy room, she finds she knows what happened but is unable to find the words to describe it. The memory exists not as a narrative but as a series of stark, disconnected images, like looking at photographs of it in her mind: the splintered wood of the market stalls, the panicked face of a woman clutching a child, the flat, metallic glint of the soldiers' rifles. And most potently, the smell. When she thinks about that day, she can sometimes smell the thick, acrid scent of sweat and fear that filled the air as everyone was herded into the sweltering warehouse.

This sensory echo haunts her daily life. A crowded elevator at her downtown office building, thick with the smell of body odour on a summer day, can send a jolt of panic through her, forcing her to exit on the next floor and wait for an empty one. The trigger is not just external; any internal sense of peace feels equally dangerous. Moments of genuine happiness or relaxation, like sitting on the porch with Tane on a Sunday morning, are the most treacherous. A wave of calm will wash over her, and immediately a secondary, colder wave of dread follows. She has come to believe that letting her guard down is an invitation for disaster, just as the placid morning market was shattered in an instant. This fear has hollowed out her emotional life, leaving her with the profound conviction that she will never be able to feel normal emotions again. The joy she sees on other people's faces feels like a foreign language she can no longer speak.

Over the decades, her world has shrunk to accommodate her fear. At her auditing firm, she has arranged her office so her desk is always against the wall, allowing her an unobstructed view of the door. She feels a primal sense of being unsafe unless she can see the whole room, a rule she applies to restaurants, waiting rooms, and family gatherings. Walking the few blocks from the bus stop to her office is an exercise in hypervigilance; she constantly glances behind her, certain she is being followed. Before any interaction at work, even a simple query to a junior colleague, she must rehearse what to say, terrified that if she doesn't, her inner turmoil will become visible. She carries a deep, pervasive shame, a feeling that others can see what happened to her just by looking at her, as if the trauma were a physical stain on her skin.

To cope, she retreats into her mind, but finds no solace there. Long, sleepless nights are spent ruminating, turning the events of that day over and over, trying to pinpoint a moment where she could have done something differently to prevent it. The question of why it happened to her has become a constant, grinding internal monologue with no answer. In a strange paradox, the woman who so carefully avoids any perceived threat will sometimes go for long walks late at night through unfamiliar neighbourhoods, a risky behaviour that offers a fleeting, perverse sense of control. It is in these moments, courting a tangible danger, that the intangible terror recedes for a moment.

The birth of her first great-grandchild six months ago brought this long-simmering crisis to a head. Holding the baby, surrounded by the uncomplicated joy of her family, she felt nothing but a profound and terrifying emptiness. The happiness around her was so complete, and her distance from it so absolute, that it cemented a thought that had been growing for years: that her life was not sure it was worth living anymore. It was this stark realisation, the fear of her own despair, that finally prompted her to seek help. She sits in the chair, her back pressed firmly into it, knowing the whole story is inside her but able to offer only its fragments, hoping to find the words that have been lost for half a century.
